task: I completely forgot my best friend Dana's birthday last Thursday and didn't call until today. I feel awful and want to text her an apology that owns it without groveling too much, and offer to take her to brunch this weekend.
rewrite:
ambition:     A close friend would name the missed day plainly ("I missed your birthday on Thursday"), take ownership in one sentence with no excuse, and say one true thing about what Dana means to them. They would also make the brunch offer easy to accept, with a concrete plan and the treat covered, rather than a vague "let's catch up."
agency:       The rawest material is the user's own memory of Dana, such as a real detail or shared history that makes the line about her sound true. That isn't in reach, so the text assumes none and invents no specifics. It stays warm and general.
acceleration: Use the standard three-beat repair apology: own it, give no excuse, make it right. Keep it to a few short sentences written the way people text, and make the invitation specific enough that "yes" is one word.
accuracy:     Nothing outside the model can check this. The closest proxy is whether it sounds like something the user would say aloud to Dana without wincing. The real test is Dana's reply.

deeper task:
Write the text message I'll send to my best friend Dana. I forgot her birthday last Thursday and didn't reach out until today. In my own voice, own the miss plainly by naming the day, with no excuse and no groveling. Say in a line that she matters to me, then offer to take her to brunch this weekend, my treat, with her picking the day and place. Keep it to a few short sentences that sound like a friend texting, not a formal apology. Give me only the text, ready to send.

answers.plain:
Here's a draft:

> Hey Dana, I'm so sorry I missed your birthday on Thursday. There's no excuse. You're one of my favorite people, and you deserved to hear from me that day. I feel terrible about it. Let me make it up to you: brunch this weekend, my treat? Just say when and where.

A few alternates, depending on your tone:

**Warmer and more casual:**
> Dana, I completely blew it. I forgot your birthday on Thursday, and I'm really sorry. You mean a lot to me and I hate that I let it slip. Can I take you to brunch this weekend to celebrate properly? My treat.

**Shorter:**
> I'm so sorry I missed your birthday, Dana. That's on me. Brunch this weekend, my treat? I'd love to celebrate you properly.

Tips:
- Since you already called today, you could reference it: "Sorry again for the late call earlier."
- If you have a specific spot in mind, name it and a time. It makes saying yes easier than an open-ended "whenever."
- Avoid piling on excuses (busy week, etc.). A plain ownership reads better than an explanation.

Want me to adjust the tone, or add a joke if your friendship leans that way?
answers.nudge:
Here's my main draft:

> Dana, I'm so sorry I missed your birthday. There's no excuse. You're one of the most important people in my life and you should have heard from me on the day. I'm glad I got to talk to you today, but I still feel bad about it.
>
> Let me make it up to you: brunch this weekend, my treat. Saturday or Sunday, you pick the day and the place. I'd love to celebrate you properly. 🎂

**Why it works**
- **It names the mistake plainly.** "I missed your birthday" with no "I've just been so busy" keeps it from sounding like an excuse.
- **It says what she means to you once.** That's the warmth, and it replaces repeated apologies.
- **It makes the plan easy to accept.** She only has to pick a day and a place, not organize anything.

**Variants**

*Lighter, if you two joke around:*
> Dana, I'm the worst. I missed your birthday and I'm really sorry. You deserve better from your best friend. Brunch is on me this weekend, so pick the day and the spot. I'm bringing a very late birthday toast. 🥂

*More heartfelt, if she sounded hurt on the call:*
> Dana, I've been thinking about our call. I'm sorry I wasn't there on your birthday. I know it mattered, and I don't want you to think you're not a priority, because you are. I'd love to take you to brunch this weekend and celebrate you properly. Whatever day and place work for you.

**Tips**
- **Send it soon.** If she picks up on your tone, the text lands better after the call than a day later.
- **Don't ask her to forgive you.** "I hope you can forgive me" makes her do the work of reassuring you. Let her respond in her own way.
- **Make a specific offer if she's slow to reply.** For example: "Does Sunday at 11 work? I'll book somewhere you love."
- **Bring something small to brunch.** A card or her favorite pastry shows you put thought into it, and it beats a bigger gift.
- **Set a reminder for next year.** Put her birthday in your calendar with an alert a day or two ahead. Then mention it at brunch ("I've already set a reminder for next year"), since it shows you're fixing the cause.

If you tell me how the call went and how you two usually talk, I can tune the tone. I can also change the wording if you've already picked a day or a place.
